blocks.p: It made him the offer on the second night, in the small hours, in the one place he had not expected it. His own kitchen. The cold kettle, the table, the chair, the exact geometry of the morning everything started. The Healer had spent a month in Gin's memories, and it knew precisely which room would do the most work for it.

Gin sat across from him in his own body, and the evenness in him was total and gentle. It laid the offer out the way it laid everything out, itemized and true, each line a thing Rei could not argue with because each line was real. "You found the Axis," it said, almost tender. "Then you know there must be a thirteenth. You know the wound will not close by itself. And you know Kishin will tear it open whether I take the chair or not. So let me make you an honest offer. The first one anyone has made you since this kitchen."

Then it did the thing Rei had not seen coming, the thing that turned the whole month inside out. It offered him the chair. Not as a threat. Not as a trap he could name. As mercy, itemized. "The seat is not particular about who fills it," it said. "It wants only to be filled by something that can hold the difference. I am built for it. But you, Rei. Two paths, held down your whole life precisely because they were strong enough to need holding down. You could hold it too. Take the Thirteenth Domain yourself, and the wound closes around you instead of me. Your brother is set down whole the moment it does, because I will no longer need him. You would stop being a witness with no grade. You would become the law the whole registered world has scrambled to stand in for. You would have saved the district, and saved Gin. And the only cost is the one thing you have spent your life refusing to pick up."

It was the most reasonable offer anyone had ever made him, and it was built entirely of true things. Rei sat in the chair from the morning everything started and felt the exact angle at which it drowned. Because it was not lying. He probably could take the seat. The wall probably would close. Gin probably would be set down whole. And the thing it did not itemize, because it did not need to, because it knew he could already feel it, was what became of the person who held the difference. There was no climbing back up from a Domain. Rei had seen the man at the hub. The load was permanent and total and not human. He would save his brother by becoming a pressure with a name Gin almost knew, a law instead of a brother, eyes in a dark room that Gin could feel and never again sit across a kitchen table from. It offered him everyone's life but his own. It offered it gently, and it meant it, and that was the worst part. The kindest exit in the structure was the one where he stopped, forever, being someone Gin could come home to.

Gin surfaced while the offer was still warm on the table. The real one, coming up through the evenness for about as long as a held breath can last. Rei knew him instantly, because the mercy went out of the eyes and what came up behind it was tired and frightened and entirely Gin. He could not hold it long. He spent what he had on the only things that mattered, fast, the way a man speaks underwater.

"Don't take it," he said. His hand found the edge of the table the way it had found the receiver, and tapped. Once, then once, then once. The widow's altar. The knock from the inside. Telling Rei in the code he had taught him that this was true, and not the Healer wearing truth like a coat. "It's not lying to you. That's how I know not to let you say yes. It would do it. It would set me down. And I would have to live in a city you became the underside of."

He told Rei the thing he had been trying to tap out since the first lucid window, the thing the Healer could not let him finish in words. He got most of it out in the broken half sentences of a man surfacing between waves. When the Healer took him, it had not taken a blank. It had taken a man who had spent his whole career writing names small in the back of a book, holding wards by committee, doing the plain load-bearing work of keeping the difference shut one favour at a time. And somewhere in a month of being worn, he had come to understand the chair from inside the thing that wanted it. There was a way to deny it to both demons. He had not been allowed to say it aloud and could not, even now, with the leash this tight. He could only give Rei the edge of it.

"The chair doesn't need a new occupant," he managed. "It needs its old one. The torn-out thing isn't gone, Rei. It was put somewhere. I helped put it. We all did, the whole registered world, that's what the wards are..."

And the leash pulled, the way a captor's leash always pulls hardest the instant the captive sees it. The evenness came back into the eyes like water closing over a swimmer, and Gin was gone again mid-word. The Healer sat across from Rei in his body with its gentle, terrible patience. It had heard every syllable. It knew now exactly how much his brother understood, and exactly how much he had managed to give away before the wave took him.

Rei sat with three knocks fading on the table and a half sentence and the nights running out. His brother had just spent what might be his last lucid strength, not on being saved, but on handing Rei the one thing the structure had not shown him at the Axis. The wound had an old occupant. And Rei had seen him. A man at the hub with his back to the world, who had sat in the Duty chair first and never fully stood up. It was a person once. The archive notes say so. The whole registered world had put him somewhere. It had put him inside a name. The Architect. A mechanism. Register XIII, null-emotive. Every ward in the city leaned its weight on him and called him a law of nature so that nobody would have to remember he had been a man. That was the lock. And the only one who could tell Rei how to open it was the man himself, who answered one question per approach and only to those who reached all the way in.

The CVD building was a grey block a minute from the east exit of Ōji station, set on the thinnest point of the ward on purpose, and Rei walked into it on the third afternoon of Obon with paper lanterns still sagging over the intake desk. Okada Shizuka came down to the lobby herself. She looked at his face, then at his hands, the way she always did.
"Gin told me to watch for you," she said. "I've been watching. Come on."

He told her in the lift, as plainly as he could. The Axis. The man at the hub. The half sentence. He needed to go through, bodily, and come back, and he needed a door that the Healer's rats could not follow and the Division's instruments could not read. Okada listened with her three notebooks pressed to her chest and did not interrupt. When the doors opened on the third sub-level she did not step out at once.
"I'll show you what there is," she said. "Then you choose. I won't choose for you."

She walked him the long way, and he understood later that she had meant him to see it. They passed a wide window onto the Training Hall. There were mats on the floor and ward-lines burned black into the boards, and at the far end a low-class spirit on a tether, a smear of cold the new ones took turns practising their reading on. The trainees were young. Seventeen, most of them. One of them said something and the rest burst out laughing, the loud, specific laughter of frightened people covering for it, and an instructor told them to settle down without much heat. "They teach the half that keeps the institution comfortable," Okada said. "Your brother used to say that. He wrote the other half down."

They passed the Sigil Room, and Rei smelled it before he saw it. Sumi and blood. Long benches, master hands, the scratch of brush on washi the only sound. At the back of the room a curtain hung across a single bench. "That's where they make an operative into someone the registry can't read," Okada said, low. "You don't watch them work, and you don't choose the artist. Gin learned his own keying so he'd never have to sit there again." She kept walking.

blocks.cap: The Mirror Room, which never closes

blocks.p: There was a door with no window and a Surveillance seal, and a faint sound behind it like birds in a far-off tree. "The Mirror Room," Okada said, without slowing. "I told you about it once. Now you know what the mirrors are bound to. Every one of them a crow somebody fed for three days." She did not look at the door. "It never closes." She tilted her head at the next door along, which had a number and nothing else. "And that one is Special Cases. That's where the possession that should not work goes, and the operative who came back wrong. They study them gently and everyone calls it care." She stopped then, and looked at him. "Ask me how many people have gone where you want to go. Then ask me how many came back right. Most of the ones who came back at all came back wrong, Rei. Some of them are very calm about it. One of them gardens. It's in the file."
Rei did not answer. She nodded as if he had, and opened a door at the end of the corridor that ought to have opened onto a stairwell.

blocks.cap: The walled green three floors underground

blocks.p: It opened onto grass. A walled green under an open sky, impossible three floors underground, with a sparring circle worn down to dirt in the middle of it. At the far end, where the instructors could see and the new ones could not, two mediums were working live against each other, one of them on her knees and getting up again. "Channel rank and above for that," Okada said. "Forms for everybody else. You leave here knowing what your ability does when a hand is genuinely trying to end you." Along one wall stood an aviary, all racket and crow-squabble, and on a perch at its end sat a falcon with a hood pushed back off its head. It turned its eyes on Rei and held them. He had the clear sense of being seen on both sides of the wall at once. "It can see the veil," Okada said. "Trained. It frightened your brother more than the sparring did."

blocks.cap: The cattery, five cats on five cushions

blocks.p: The last door was warm. The room behind it smelled of clean straw and old paper. Five cats lay on five cushions, each with a small brass tag. Sera. Itou. Mochida. Hara. Kuga. "Names of five operatives who didn't come back," Okada said quietly. "The handler named the cats for them." The senior handler was a woman who did not give her name and did not look up from the cat in her lap. Kuga was on the cushion by the window, a big grey animal with torn ears, and he did not look up either.
Okada sat Rei down on a crate and laid it out.

"There are two ways for someone like you to put his body through and get it back," she said. "The first is the False Death. Pufferfish toxin and snake venom, mixed to a ratio the archive keeps. Forty-eight hours to prepare it, no less. The person going under needs Psychometabolism at the third level, and a second person with it at the second level has to sit the watch and run the return. You hold an object against your breastbone, something you've carried more than a year, so your soul can find the body again. Three to seven minutes and you have no pulse. To anything below Class A you read as dead. Your consciousness waits at the Threshold. The window to bring you back is three or four hours. Nobody has come back after eight." She paused. "There's one death on record from doing it without a monitor. And the Threshold is not empty. Things there can reach a soul held that close to the door."
"I don't have Psychometabolism," Rei said. "And I don't have forty-eight hours."

"No." She looked at the window cushion. "The second way is a cat. Still water at least two centimetres deep, still enough to be a mirror. You stand in it barefoot. You hold the cat against your chest with both hands. You look into its eyes and you do not look away. Rank doesn't come into it. The cat's pupil is the aperture. If it consents, and it takes ten seconds to forty for it to decide, its weight changes in your hands and the room behind it stops being the room. That's the door. Your sight goes up a tier. You can step partway through, or with a cat that knows the way, much further. The cat chooses the distance. Not you. It costs you eight points of stability to open. It holds fifteen to thirty minutes. Nobody has held one past forty. When the cat looks away, the door shuts, at once, with no warning." She turned back to him. "To our instruments you'll read as a stray cat and nothing else. That's why it's the cleanest crossing there is. But it doesn't make you invisible to anything already on the other side. Know the difference."

"I cross through Kuga and no other when it truly matters," the handler said, still without looking up. "But he's not mine to lend. Access is the handler and the cat's consent. The cat's consent outranks me."

blocks.cap: Kuga, the grey cat with the torn ears

blocks.p: Kuga opened his eyes. He got down off his cushion without hurry, the way cats do everything, and crossed the straw, and sat at Rei's feet. Then he looked up into Rei's face and kept looking.
The handler let out a breath. "Well," she said. "That's that, then."

Okada signed the cat out on a clipboard by the door, under her own name, and Rei watched her do it and knew exactly what rule she was breaking and how much she would hate herself for it later. She did not say anything about it. She only said, "The node behind the Senju waterworks. Gin marked it smallest. The smallest tear is the one most likely to let a living man back out. I'll meet you there after dark with the water."

The third night came the way the bottom of a held breath comes. Rei stood at the seam in Kita with a cat carrier at his feet, and below him the first sending-fires were being lit, early, in the old streets, the way Kita lit everything early now. Okuribi, the gentle farewell. Small flames guiding the dead back to the other side, every one of them a family's tenderness, and every one of them, this year, a fraction of the pull the Healer had spent a month preparing to borrow. He could feel the hinge through his two opened paths. The great seasonal lean of the world was beginning to turn from welcome to farewell. And at the pitch of each small swing the curtain over the wound went from thin to almost nothing, and he could feel how it would be on the last night, when the swing was total and the door stood open in both directions at once.

Kishin was already leaning into the gap, hunger made weather, its mouth somewhere in the dark below with Kaito's young face. The Healer was already climbing, Gin's body carrying it toward the place where the chair would be, with the calm of an appointment it meant to keep. And Rei stood between them at the wound with everything he had learned and no law of his own. The structure waited, with the patience it had had since before the wards had names, for him to choose which fire the night would light.

He understood, standing there with the okuribi burning under him, that this had never been a puzzle with a solution. There was no move that saved everything. The Axis had shown him that, and the offer in the kitchen had proved it. Every way off this embankment cost something. Trust the monster in his brother's body and stake the district on its mercy. Throw himself against the wound and hope his mind lasted longer than the night. Take Gin's hand and walk away and let the lanterns go out over a ward that had lit them early. He could feel each of them the way he could feel the slope, and none of them was clean. Only one thing in the whole structure was not already decided, and it was the half sentence his brother had drowned to give him. It needs its old one.

The sending-fires burned. The hinge swung. His brother climbed toward the chair, and somewhere under the evenness a held breath of his own was still knocking, once, then once, then once. Whatever Rei chose, he would choose it for all of it. The wall, the district, the chair, the man, and the person he would be on the far side of this, who was not the person who had stood in a cold kitchen a few nights and a whole life ago and counted the doors the morning had left open. The structure would not decide for him. The demons could not. And Gin, drowned and knocking, had spent everything he had to leave it in his hands.

Rei took the breath the city was letting go of. He did not choose the fire yet. He chose the door. Before he chose anything for all of it, he would go down and ask the old occupant the one question he was allowed. He picked up the carrier, and Kuga shifted inside it, and he went down off the seam toward the river and the waterworks, where Okada was waiting with the water.
